content: The databases Medline, Embase, and Google Scholar were systematically searched to identify peer-reviewed journal articles published before September 6, 2021. No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, conference proceedings from four major hepatitis meetings and grey literature were reviewed. To ensure comprehensive coverage, bibliographic references of relevant full-text papers were manually searched. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) they reported on HCV viral load reflex laboratory-based testing; (2) they involved the general adult population (aged >18 years) or key subpopulations at increased risk of HCV infection, such as people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, and sex workers; and (3) they provided raw data on at least one aspect of the HCV care continuum. Outcomes assessed included time from antibody testing to RNA testing, time from RNA sample collection to RNA testing, time from RNA testing to results availability, time from RNA testing to treatment initiation, and time from antibody testing to treatment initiation. Data were also extracted from studies reporting on clinic-based reflex testing, including those from a review on HCV point-of-care (PoC) viral load testing. Results were reported separately for laboratory-based and clinic-based reflex testing. Forest plots were generated to display odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for the main findings, and random-effects models were used to summarize estimates. A total of 10,750 citations were screened, with 30 additional citations identified through reference screening. Ultimately, 51 studies were included in the analysis. Of these, 18 (35%) were conducted in the United States, 9 (18%) in Spain, and 5 (10%) in the United Kingdom. Only 9 studies (18%) were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, while 42 (82%) were conducted in high-income countries. Among the included studies, 16 (31%) focused on people who inject drugs and homeless populations, 7 (14%) on baby boomers, 6 (12%) on HCV-positive populations, 6 (12%) on hospital patients, and 13 (25%) on the general or mixed populations. Of the included studies, 32 (63%) utilized laboratory-based reflex testing, while 19 (37%) used clinic-based reflex testing. Nine of the 32 laboratory-based reflex testing studies included a non-reflex comparison group, whereas none of the clinic-based reflex testing studies had a non-reflex comparator group. All included studies were either cross-sectional or cohort studies; none were randomized controlled trials. Risk of bias was assessed as high in 26 studies (51%), moderate in 11 studies (22%), and low in 14 studies (27%). Most studies (42 of 51, 82%) were published after 2018. For laboratory-based reflex testing, 96% (95% CI: 92–98%) of patients screened as antibody-positive initiated HCV RNA testing using this strategy. Among these, 58% (95% CI: 49–66%) were diagnosed with HCV infection, 77% (95% CI: 71–83%) were linked to care, and 45% (95% CI: 31–61%) initiated HCV treatment. In contrast, for laboratory-based non-reflex testing, 68% (95% CI: 52–82%) of antibody-positive patients initiated RNA testing, 63% (95% CI: 48–76%) were diagnosed with HCV infection, 63% (95% CI: 29–92%) were linked to care, and 67% (95% CI: 42–88%) initiated treatment. Turnaround times for laboratory-based reflex testing were significantly reduced, with the time from antibody testing to reflex sampling reduced to 0 days. The time from RNA sample collection to viral load testing ranged from 1 to 3 days, while the time from RNA testing to results availability ranged from 1 to 14 days. The time from RNA testing to treatment initiation ranged from 52 to 83 days. For clinic-based reflex testing, 94% (95% CI: 85–99%) of antibody-positive patients initiated RNA testing, 67% (95% CI: 57–76%) were diagnosed with HCV infection, and 84% (95% CI: 79–87%) initiated treatment. Turnaround times for clinic-based reflex testing were also reduced, with a median time of 0 days for RNA sample collection to viral load testing in 10 studies, 1 day in 2 studies, and 5 days in 1 study. The time from RNA testing to treatment initiation ranged from 0 to 57 days. HCV viral load reflex testing, whether laboratoryor clinic-based, demonstrated significant advantages over non-reflex testing strategies. These included reduced turnaround times, increased viral load testing rates, improved linkage to care, and higher treatment initiation rates. Reflex testing strategies are feasible and have the potential for widespread adoption, even in resource-limited settings, to promote HCV treatment uptake. This systematic review and meta-analysis support the use of laboratoryor clinic-based reflex testing as an alternative to conventional multi-step laboratory-based diagnostic strategies. Reflex testing enables prompt linkage to care and treatment initiation, which is critical for achieving global HCV elimination targets.
